claim: Memories encoded in the dentate gyrus (DG) – CA3 circuit of the hippocampus are routed from CA1 to anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) for consolidation.
source: Memories encoded in the dentate gyrus (DG) ‒ CA3 circuit of the hippocampus are routed from CA1 to anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) for consolidation.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established understanding of memory consolidation pathways in the hippocampal-cortical network.

claim: CA1 parvalbumin inhibitory neurons (PV INs) orchestrate hippocampal-cortical communication.
source: Although CA1 parvalbumin inhibitory neurons (PV INs) orchestrate hippocampal-cortical communication, we know less about CA3 PV INs or DG ‒ CA3 principal neuron ‒ IN circuit mechanisms that contribute to evolution of hippocampal-cortical ensembles during memory consolidation.
evidence: This statement references prior research on CA1 PV INs and their role in hippocampal-cortical communication.

claim: FFI facilitates formation and maintenance of context-associated neuronal ensembles in CA1.
source: Using viral genetics to selectively mimic and boost an endogenous learning-dependent circuit mechanism, DG cell recruitment of CA3 PV INs and feed-forward inhibition (FFI) in CA3, in combination with longitudinal in vivo calcium imaging, we demonstrate that FFI facilitates formation and maintenance of context-associated neuronal ensembles in CA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from longitudinal calcium imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing FFI in DG – CA3 promoted context specificity of neuronal ensembles in ACC over time.
source: Increasing FFI in DG ‒ CA3 promoted context specificity of neuronal ensembles in ACC over time and enhanced long-term contextual fear memory.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on calcium imaging data showing ensemble properties in ACC.

claim: Increasing FFI in DG – CA3 enhanced long-term contextual fear memory.
source: Increasing FFI in DG ‒ CA3 promoted context specificity of neuronal ensembles in ACC over time and enhanced long-term contextual fear memory.
evidence: This finding is based on behavioral data from contextual fear conditioning experiments.

claim: Enhanced CA1 sharp-wave ripple – ACC spindle coupling is a potential network mechanism facilitating memory consolidation.
source: In vivo LFP recordings in mice with increased FFI in DG ‒ CA3 identified enhanced CA1 sharp-wave ripple ‒ ACC spindle coupling as a potential network mechanism facilitating memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim is based on in vivo LFP recordings showing enhanced ripple-spindle coupling.

claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in the formation of new episodic memories by generating conjunctive representations of experiences.
source: The hippocampus plays a critical role in the formation of new episodic memories by generating conjunctive representations of experiences and transferring these representations to neocortical sites for memory storage or consolidation (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005; McClelland et al., 1995; Peyrache et al., 2009; Squire, 2004; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research on hippocampal function in memory.

claim: Prefrontal cortical neuronal ensembles undergo time-dependent refinement and re-organization as memories transition from recent to remote configurations.
source: Following learning, prefrontal cortical neuronal ensembles are thought to undergo time-dependent refinement and re-organization as memories transition from recent to remote configurations and become more generalized (DeNardo et al., 2019; Frankland and Bontempi, 2005; Frankland et al., 2004; Maviel et al., 2004; McClelland et al., 1995; Morrissey et al., 2017; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008; Wiltgen et al., 2010; Winocur et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on memory consolidation.

claim: The hippocampus plays a sustained role in remote memory retrieval.
source: Indeed, a growing body of experimental evidence not only supports a sustained role for the hippocampus in remote memory retrieval (Goshen et al., 2011; Vetere et al., 2021) but also in dictating the extent to which remote memories retain contextual details of the original experience (Guo et al., 2018; Koolschijn et al., 2019; Tompary and Davachi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Genetic silencing of engram-bearing dentate granule neurons post training impaired the maturation of context-specific neuronal ensembles in prefrontal cortex.
source: Specifically, genetic silencing of engram-bearing dentate granule neurons post training was shown to impair the maturation of context-specific neuronal ensembles in prefrontal cortex (Kitamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Chronic genetic inhibition of CA3 outputs impaired high-frequency network oscillations such as sharp-wave ripples.
source: Chronic genetic inhibition of CA3 outputs impaired high-frequency network oscillations such as sharp-wave ripples, experience-related firing patterns in CA1 and long-term contextual fear memory (Nakashiba et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CA1 PV INs promote sharp-wave ripples (SWR) and facilitate hippocampal-cortical communication through increased sharp-wave ripple – spindle coupling in CA1 – ACC networks.
source: CA1 PV INs have been shown to orchestrate synchronous activation of principal neurons, promote sharp-wave ripples (SWR), and facilitate hippocampal-cortical communication through increased sharp-wave ripple ‒ spindle coupling in CA1 ‒ ACC networks (Buzsáki, 2015; Çaliskan et al., 2016; Gan et al., 2016; Ognjanovski et al., 2017; Stark et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PV INs in CA1 or in ACC following training inhibited consolidation of contextual fear memory.
source: Chemogenetic inhibition of PV INs in CA1 or in ACC following training inhibited consolidation of contextual fear memory (Ognjanovski et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dentate granule cell recruitment of feed-forward inhibition (FFI) onto CA3 is temporarily enhanced following learning.
source: Dentate granule cell recruitment of feed-forward inhibition (FFI) onto CA3 is temporarily enhanced following learning and is one inhibitory circuit mechanism linked to memory consolidation (Guo et al., 2018; Ruediger et al., 2012; Ruediger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Viral mediated selective enhancement of dentate granule cell recruitment of PV INs in CA3 increased inhibition onto CA3 and enhanced strength and precision of remote memories.
source: In previous work, we found that viral mediated selective enhancement of dentate granule cell recruitment of PV INs in CA3 increased inhibition onto CA3 and enhanced strength and precision of remote memories (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Increasing FFI in DG – CA3 conferred context-specific reactivation of neuronal ensembles in hippocampal – ACC – basolateral amygdala networks at remote timepoints.
source: Using genetic ensemble-tagging approaches and immediate-early gene expression, we found that increasing FFI in DG ‒ CA3 conferred context-specific reactivation of neuronal ensembles in hippocampal ‒ ACC ‒ basolateral amygdala networks at remote timepoints.
evidence: This claim is based on prior work by the authors using genetic ensemble-tagging approaches.

claim: Maintenance of engram-bearing cell connectivity with PV INs prevented the time-dependent decay of the hippocampal engram.
source: Furthermore, we found that maintenance of engram-bearing cell connectivity with PV INs prevented the time-dependent decay of the hippocampal engram thereby suggesting a link between maintenance of the hippocampal memory trace and remote memory precision (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on prior work by the authors.

claim: Injection of lenti-shRNA into dentate gyrus increased MFT filopodia onto PV INs.
source: Injection of lenti-shRNA into dentate gyrus (DG) increased MFT filopodia onto PV INs.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Injection of lenti-shRNA significantly increased PV puncta in CA3.
source: Injection of lenti-shRNA significantly increased PV puncta in CA3 [Two-tailed Mann-Whitney: p = 0.029, n = 4] but not in CA1 [Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, layer x virus effect p = 0.583: virus main effect p = 0.752, layer main effect: p < 0.0001]; or ACC [Two-tailed Mann-Whitney test: p = 0.886, n = 4].
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1b with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a significantly higher number of PV puncta in the deeper layer of CA1 compared to the superficial layer.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018), we found a significantly higher number of PV puncta in the deeper layer of CA1 compared to the superficial layer [Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, layer x virus effect: N.S.: main virus effect N.S., main layer effect p < 0.0001, n = 4].
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data and a citation to prior research.

claim: The viral manipulation did not affect PV puncta in CA1 or ACC.
source: Our manipulation did not affect PV puncta in CA1 or ACC [ACC: Two-tailed Mann-Whitney test: N.S., n = 4] (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Both groups of mice responded similarly to foot-shocks in the training context A.
source: Behavioral analysis of freezing levels revealed that both groups of mice responded similarly to foot-shocks in the training context A (Figure 2a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A subset of neurons in both CA1 and ACC exhibited significant elevation in activity in response to foot-shocks (Foot-shock responsive neurons or FSR neurons) in both groups of mice.
source: Consistent with prior work (Jimenez et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020), our recordings of calcium transients during contextual fear conditioning revealed a subset of neurons in both CA1 and ACC that exhibited significant elevation in activity in response to foot-shocks (Foot-shock responsive neurons or FSR neurons) in both groups of mice [Two-tailed paired t-test, ACC shNT preFS vs postFS: p = 0.004, n = 5, ACC shRNA preFS vs postFS: p = 0.013, n = 5, CA1 shNT preFS vs postFS: p = 0.007, n = 5, CA1 shRNA preFS vs postFS: p = 0.024, n = 5](Figure 2b, d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data with statistical analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: The fraction of FSR neurons in ACC was significantly increased in the shRNA group compared to shNT group.
source: However, the fraction of FSR neurons in ACC was significantly increased in the shRNA group compared to shNT group [Two-tailed unpaired t-test with Welch's correction, p = 0.043, n = 5] (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in FSR neuron activity in CA1 and ACC was accompanied by an increase in co-activity of these neurons.
source: Further analysis of FSR neurons revealed that the increase in FSR neuron activity in CA1 and ACC was accompanied by an increase in co-activity of these neurons i.e. increase in number of FSR correlated pairs [Two-tailed paired t-test, ACC shNT: p = 0.021, n = 5, ACC shRNA: N.S., n = 5, CA1 shNT: p = 0.021, n = 5, CA1 shRNA: p = 0.001, n = 5] (Figure 2g–h and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The shRNA mice exhibited a significantly higher increase in correlated neurons in CA1 mice.
source: Additionally, the shRNA mice exhibited a significantly higher increase in correlated neurons in CA1 mice [Two-tailed unpaired t-test with Welch's correction, p = 0.044, n = 5] (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data with statistical analysis.

claim: Both shRNA and shNT groups exhibited high levels of discrimination of the two contexts one day following fear conditioning.
source: Behavioral analysis revealed that both shRNA and shNT groups exhibited high levels of discrimination of the two contexts and showed similar levels of freezing in training context A and negligible levels of freezing in context C [Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, treatment x time effect N.S., time main effect p = 0.014; treatment main effect N.S.; n = 10, pooled ACC and CA1 mice. see Figure 3—figure supplement 3c for separate ACC and CA1 data] (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: Both virus groups showed increased numbers of correlated neurons compared to baseline levels only in context A and not in the novel, distinct neutral context C.
source: Specifically, both virus groups showed increased numbers of correlated neurons compared to baseline levels only in context A and not in the novel, distinct neutral context C (yet non-significant in shRNA mice) [one sample t-test against 1 (BL), context A, shNT: p = 0.003, n = 5, shRNA: N.S. (strong trend, p = 0.055), n = 5; context C: shNT: N.S., n = 5, shRNA: N.S., n = 5] (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The shRNA group showed a significant increase in number of correlated pairs in ACC in context A indicative of emergence of a training context-associated ensemble in ACC.
source: Additionally, in context A, the shRNA group also showed a significant increase in number of correlated pairs in ACC indicative of emergence of a training context-associated ensemble in ACC [one sample t-test against 1 (BL), context A, ACC, shNT: N.S., shRNA: p = 0.018, n = 5] (Figure 3c–d)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis with statistical testing.

claim: There was no reactivation of FSR neurons among the correlated pairs of neurons identified in CA1 in the recall session.
source: Using CellReg (Sheintuch et al., 2017) to register neurons across sessions, we found no reactivation of FSR neurons among the correlated pairs of neurons identified in CA1 in the recall session [shNT: mean: 0.0 S.E.M. 0; shRNA: mean 0.0, S.E.M, 0] (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on cell registration analysis across sessions.

claim: There was no correlation between the number of correlated neuronal pairs and the time mice moved in the respective context.
source: We controlled for the possible effect of locomotion on neuronal activity by quantifying the time mice moved in each context and found no correlation between the number of correlated neuronal pairs and the time mice moved in the respective context [Pearson's correlation, ACC context A, R2 = 0.19, p = 0.196, ACC context C: R2 = 0.00, p = 0.935, CA1 context A: R2 = 0.09, p = 0.376, CA1 context C: R2 = 0.04, p = 0.599, n = 5 mice per group] (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-d).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between locomotion and neuronal activity.

claim: Neurons in CA1 showed higher activity in context C relative to context A.
source: Neurons in CA1 (including A&C neurons) showed higher activity i.e. rate of calcium transients in context C relative to context A [Two-way ANOVA with repeated measures, CA1, shNT: context x time effect p < 0.0001, time main effect p = 0.007, context main effect p = 0.028, n = 5; shRNA,: context x time effect p < 0.0001, time main effect p = 0.012, context main effect p = 0.029, n = 5] [A&C neurons: one sample t-test against 0, CA1, shNT: p = 0.007, shRNA: p = 0.048, n = 5] suggestive of a novelty response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1i-j, Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data with statistical analysis.

claim: The shRNA group showed significantly fewer A&C neurons in CA1 indicating that increasing FFI in DG – CA3 reduced the number of neurons that were active in both contexts.
source: Interestingly, the shRNA group showed significantly fewer A&C neurons in CA1 indicating that increasing FFI in DG ‒ CA3 reduced the number of neurons that were active in both contexts [Two-tailed unpaired t-test with Welch's correction, p = 0.048, n = 5] (Figure 3h).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of A&C neurons with statistical analysis.

claim: The shRNA group exhibited significantly higher levels of discrimination between the two contexts than the shNT group at 16 days following training.
source: Behavioral analysis revealed that the shRNA group exhibited significantly higher levels of discrimination between the two contexts than the shNT group [Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, treatment x time effect N.S., treatment main effect: p = 0.028, n = 10, see Figure 3—figure supplement 3d for comparison of ACC and CA1] (Figure 3j).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: Both groups of mice maintained an increase in correlated pairs in CA1 during recall in context A at day 16.
source: Both groups of mice maintained an increase in correlated pairs in CA1 during recall in context A (two-tailed unpaired student's t-test with Welch's correction, N .S., n = 5), however the shRNA group did not exhibit a significant decrease in correlated pairs from day 1 to day 16 as seen for shNT group (Two-tailed paired t-test, shNT p = 0.041, shRNA: N.S. n = 5, comparison not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The shRNA group showed increased co-activity in context C at day 16 that was significantly higher compared to shNT group.
source: Furthermore, the shRNA group showed increased co-activity in context C [One-sample t-test against 1 (baseline, BL), context A, shNT, p = 0.006; shRNA, p = 0.04; context C, shNT p = N .S.; shRNA, p = 0.026; n = 5;] that was significantly higher compared to shNT group in context C [two-tailed unpaired student's t-test with welch correction, p = 0.042, n = 5] (Figure 3k).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The A&C neurons in CA1 in the shRNA group exhibited higher activity in context C relative to context A at day 16.
source: We found that the A&C neurons in CA1 in the shRNA group exhibited higher activity (rate of calcium events) in context C relative to context A [one sample t-test against 0, shNT: N.S., shRNA: p = 0.012, n = 5] (Figure 3l).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data with statistical analysis.

claim: The shRNA group showed significantly fewer A&C neurons among all correlated pairs of neurons in CA1 compared to the shNT group at remote recall.
source: Furthermore, the shRNA group showed significantly fewer A&C neurons among all correlated pairs of neurons in CA1 compared to the shNT group [two-tailed unpaired t-test with Welch's correction, p = 0.017, n = 5; A&C neurons, recent, ACC, shNT 42.97 ± 8.37, shRNA 39.07 ± 5.93,CA1, shNT, 27.03 ± 8.23, shRNA, 30.64 ± 4.65; remote, ACC, shNT 33.59 ± 11.82, shRNA, 36.34 ± 12.14, CA1, shNT, 52.26 ± 4.80, shRNA, 28.55 ± 6.17; mean ± SEM] (Figure 3n and Figure 3—figure supplement 1g-h).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data with statistical analysis.

claim: The shRNA group showed significantly fewer A&C neurons in ACC at day 16 indicating that fewer neurons were active in both contexts.
source: While there was no difference in the number of A&C neurons between virus groups in CA1 [two tailed unpaired t-test with Welch's correction, N.S., n = 5], the shRNA group showed significantly fewer A&C neurons in ACC indicating that fewer neurons were active in both contexts C [two-tailed unpaired t-test with Welch's correction, p = 0.028, n = 5] (Figure 3m).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data with statistical analysis.

claim: A support vector machine trained on time-binned events in A&C neurons in CA1 performed better than shuffled data.
source: A support vector machine trained on time-binned events (5 s) in A&C neurons in CA1 performed better than shuffled data (see example distribution in Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the recent time point, day 1, calcium events in A&C neurons in both groups were sufficient to reliably predict context.
source: At the recent time point, day 1, calcium events in A&C neurons in both groups were sufficient to reliably predict context [Mann Whitney test, N .S., n = 4; One-sample t-test against 50 (chance level), shNT, p = 0.012, shRNA, p = 0.005, n = 4].
evidence: This claim is supported by decoder analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The shRNA group maintained a similarly high level of information in the A&C neurons at the remote time point.
source: The shRNA group maintained a similarly high level of information in the A&C neurons as we were able to predict the context with similar accuracy at the remote time point [One-sample t-test against 50 (chance level), shRNA, p = 0.008, n = 4].
evidence: This claim is supported by decoder analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Decoder trained on shNT mice showed a reduction in prediction accuracy for the remote time point resulting in significantly less prediction accuracy in shNT mice compared to shRNA mice.
source: In contrast, decoder trained on shNT mice showed a reduction in prediction accuracy for the remote time point resulting in significantly less prediction accuracy in shNT mice compared to shRNA mice [Mann Whitney test, p = 0.029, n = 4] (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoder analysis with statistical testing.

claim: There was a positive correlation between decoder accuracy and the ability of mice to discriminate between the two contexts.
source: We further tested if the decoder accuracy correlated with the ability of mice to discriminate between the two contexts. We found a positive correlation between these two parameters indicating that A&C neurons may indeed serve to guide context-associated behavioral responses [Pearson's correlation, shNT: R2 = 0.579, p = 0.028, n = 8, shRNA R2 = 0.577, p = 0.028, n = 8].
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between decoder accuracy and behavior.

claim: In learning naïve shRNA-injected mice, there were significantly more ripples that co-occur with spindles (coupled ripples) compared to control mice.
source: In learning naïve shRNA-injected mice, we found significantly more ripples that co-occur with spindles (coupled ripples) compared to control mice (Figure 5c, Two-tailed unpaired student's t-test with Welch's correction, p = 0.049, n = 5 per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recording data with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in coupled ripples in naïve shRNA mice was not due to an increase in ripple or spindle occurrence.
source: This was not due to an increase in ripple or spindle occurrence (Figure 5d–e) [Two-tailed unpaired student's t-test with Welch's correction, ripples/sec: N.S., n = 5 per group, spindles/sec, N.S., n = 5].
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of ripple and spindle occurrence.

claim: There was an increase in coupled ripples in control mice following contextual fear learning.
source: In line with previous studies, we found an increase in coupled ripples in control mice (Maingret et al., 2016; Xia et al., 2017) [Paired Student's t-test, p = 0.019, n = 5] to a similar level as seen in naive shRNA-injected mice (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recording data with statistical analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: Training induced an increase in overall ripple occurrence in control mice but not in shRNA mice.
source: While training induced an increase in overall ripple occurrence (ripple/sec, Figure 5g) in control mice [Paired Student's t-test, p = 0.031, n = 5], this was not seen in shRNA mice [Paired Student's t-test, N.S., n = 5].
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of ripple occurrence with statistical analysis.

claim: Increasing FFI in DG – CA3 prevents time-dependent decay of training context-associated ensemble in CA1.
source: At remote recall, we observed that FFI in DG ‒ CA3 prevented time-dependent decay of the training context-associated ensemble and promoted acquisition (or maintenance since it may have emerged prior to test at remote timepoint) of a neutral context specific ensemble in CA1 (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: This is a summary finding based on the longitudinal calcium imaging data.

claim: Increasing FFI in DG – CA3 promoted acquisition of a neutral context specific ensemble in CA1 at remote timepoint.
source: At remote recall, we observed that FFI in DG ‒ CA3 prevented time-dependent decay of the training context-associated ensemble and promoted acquisition (or maintenance since it may have emerged prior to test at remote timepoint) of a neutral context specific ensemble in CA1 (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: This is a summary finding based on the longitudinal calcium imaging data.

claim: There was a FFI dependent reduction in the number of neurons active in both training and neutral contexts in ACC at remote timepoint.
source: Within the ACC, and not evident at the recent timepoint, we observed a FFI dependent reduction in the number of neurons active in both training and neutral contexts (Figure 6b, bottom).
evidence: This is a summary finding based on the longitudinal calcium imaging data.

claim: Increasing FFI in DG – CA3 induced learning-dependent enhancement in network synchrony in CA1 – ACC in behaviorally naïve mice.
source: Electrophysiological recordings suggest that increasing FFI in DG ‒ CA3 induced learning-dependent enhancement in network synchrony in CA1 ‒ ACC in behaviorally naïve mice (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a summary finding based on the LFP recording data.

claim: The DG – CA3 circuit contributes to encoding of episodic memories conjunctive representations that relate people, objects, events with the spatial and temporal contexts in which they occur.
source: The DG ‒ CA3 circuit contributes to encoding of episodic memories conjunctive representations that relate people, objects, events with the spatial and temporal contexts in which they occur.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of the DG-CA3 circuit based on established knowledge.

claim: PV INs in CA1 and ACC are thought to mediate learning-induced synchronization of neuronal activity to stabilize memory ensembles and channel information across different regions.
source: PV INs in CA1 and ACC are thought to mediate learning-induced synchronization of neuronal activity to stabilize memory ensembles and channel information across different regions (Buzsáki, 2015; Çaliskan et al., 2016; Dupret et al., 2013; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021; Gan et al., 2016; Ognjanovski et al., 2017; Stark et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: FSR neurons found during encoding do not appear to participate in CA1 context-specific ensembles at recent recall.
source: Thus, early stages of memory consolidation are characterized by increased co-activity of neurons within CA1 as also observed previously (Ognjanovski et al., 2017) and FSR neurons found during encoding do not appear to participate in CA1 context-specific ensembles at recent recall.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis of FSR neurons and context-associated ensembles.

claim: Increasing FFI in DG – CA3 facilitated the emergence of training context-specific ensembles in CA1 and ACC suggestive of increased SWR – spindle coupling between CA1 – ACC during memory consolidation.
source: Furthermore, increasing FFI in DG ‒ CA3 facilitated the emergence of training context-specific ensembles in CA1 and ACC suggestive of increased SWR ‒ spindle coupling between CA1 ‒ ACC during memory consolidation (Maingret et al., 2016; Ognjanovski et al., 2017; Steadman et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations to prior work on SWR-spindle coupling.

claim: Increasing granule cell recruitment of perisomatic inhibition onto CA3 neurons imposes a sparser activity regimen from DG to CA3.
source: We predict that increasing granule cell recruitment of perisomatic inhibition onto CA3 neurons imposes a sparser activity regimen from DG to CA3 thereby reducing the likelihood of recruitment of the same CA3 neurons to distinct ensembles during learning (Csicsvari et al., 2000; de la Prida et al., 2006; Gómez-Ocádiz et al., 2021; Mori et al., 2007; Neubrandt et al., 2017; Sasaki et al., 2018; Torborg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the manipulation and prior research on sparse coding.

claim: Assemblies of CA3 neurons encoding different contexts entrain activity of downstream ensembles of CA1 principal neurons.
source: In turn, assemblies of CA3 neurons encoding different contexts entrain activity of downstream ensembles of CA1 principal neurons (Choi et al., 2018; Csicsvari et al., 2000; de la Prida et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Distinct ensembles in CA1 recruit local PV INs to synchronize their activity and form SWRs.
source: Distinct ensembles in CA1 recruit local PV INs to synchronize their activity and form SWRs (Choi et al., 2018; Csicsvari and Dupret, 2014; Gan et al., 2016; Malerba et al., 2017; Ognjanovski et al., 2017; Stark et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CA3 neurons that encode novel spatial information were shown to be more likely active during SWR in CA1.
source: CA3 neurons that encode novel spatial information were shown to be more likely active during SWR in CA1 suggesting that interregional maps may be strengthened during consolidation (Hwaun and Colgin, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PV INs have been implicated to regulate fidelity of spike transfer.
source: PV INs have been implicated to regulate fidelity of spike transfer (i.e. in form of coordinated spiking or burst firing of excitatory neurons) (Lamsa et al., 2005; Mori et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Feedforward inhibition in DG – CA3 synapses is naturally enhanced for several hours following learning.
source: Importantly, feedforward inhibition in DG ‒ CA3 synapses is naturally enhanced for several hours following learning (see Ruediger et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A&C neurons may function as 'schema' neurons in that they represent shared features across ensembles and facilitate the formation of new context-associated ensembles.
source: These A&C neurons may function as "schema" neurons in that they represent shared features (statistical regularities) across ensembles and facilitate the formation of new context-associated ensembles (Abdou et al., 2018; McKenzie et al., 2014; McKenzie et al., 2013; Tse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the function of A&C neurons based on prior research on schema neurons.

claim: Increased neuronal excitability has been shown to bias recruitment of neurons into ensembles.
source: Increased neuronal excitability has been shown to bias recruitment of neurons into ensembles (Yiu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CA1 balances abstraction of statistical regularities across memories mediated by the temporoammonic pathway with encoding of detail-rich distinct contextual representations conveyed through the trisynaptic EC → DG → CA3 → CA1 circuit.
source: Computational modeling has suggested that CA1 balances abstraction of statistical regularities across memories mediated by the temporoammonic pathway (EC → CA1) with encoding of detail-rich distinct contextual representations conveyed through the trisynaptic EC → DG → CA3 → CA1 circuit (Schapiro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to computational modeling work.

claim: The manipulation biases the trade-off in CA1 towards generation of context-specific ensembles over generation of schema.
source: Our data supports this model since we observe a reduction in neurons encoding overlapping features (A&C neurons) in CA1 (this study) when we increase FFI in DG ‒ CA3 and reduce interference between context associated ensembles in CA3 (Allegra et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2018; Koolschijn et al., 2019; Leutgeb et al., 2004). Thus, our manipulation biases the trade-off in CA1 towards generation of context-specific ensembles in CA1 over generation of schema.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of computational models and prior research.

claim: Reversing reductions in FFI in DG – CA3 found during aging or Alzheimer's disease may represent a strategy to restore memory consolidation.
source: While shifting this balance in healthy animals may come at a cost, reversing reductions in FFI in DG ‒ CA3 found during aging or Alzheimer's disease may represent a strategy to restore memory consolidation (Guo et al., 2018; Viana da Silva et al., 2019, Twarkowski and Sahay unpublished observations).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: CA1 plays an instructive teacher-like role in governing re-organization of ensembles in ACC during memory consolidation.
source: Our data builds on foundational theories (McClelland et al., 1995; Nadel and Moscovitch, 1997; Teyler and DiScenna, 1986; Winocur et al., 2010; Winocur et al., 2007) to suggest a continuous role for CA1 in playing an instructive teacher-like role in governing re-organization of ensembles in ACC during memory consolidation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of foundational theories.

claim: Stabilization of training-context associated ensembles in CA1 over time governs a toggle switch in the ACC that determines the extent to which memories may retain details over time.
source: We infer from our data that stabilization of training-context associated ensembles in CA1 over time governs a toggle switch in the ACC that determines the extent to which memories may retain details over time.

claim: The maintenance of the hippocampal index for an experience permits access to details of the original experience stored in distributed neocortical sites.
source: Such an interpretation is consistent with hippocampal indexing theory in that the maintenance of the hippocampal index for an experience permits access to details of the original experience stored in distributed neocortical sites (Besnard and Sahay, 2016; Goode et al., 2020; Koolschijn et al., 2019; Teyler and DiScenna, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to hippocampal indexing theory.
